calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$

onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

argument ([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A,B$ be

and define the **covariance** of the pair $(A,B)$ in the preparation $u$ by

derivations.claim: [Differentiability of $f$] By [F2], $(A\psi)'(t)=A\psi'(t)$ and both factors $A\psi(t)$ and $\psi(t)$ are $C^1$ into $\mathcal H$; the product rule for the inner product gives $f'(t)=\langle(A\psi)'(t),\psi(t)\rangle+\langle A\psi(t),\psi'(t)\rangle=\langle A\psi'(t),\psi(t)\rangle+\langle A\psi(t),\psi'(t)\rangle$.

[Bounded time-dependent observable] Let $A_t$ be a bounded self-adjoint family, $C^1$ in operator norm, and $g(t)=\langle A_t\psi(t),\psi(t)\rangle$. By the product rule for the three $C^1$ factors, $g'=\langle A'_t\psi,\psi\rangle+\langle A_t\psi',\psi\rangle+\langle A_t\psi,\psi'\rangle$; self-adjointness of $A_t$ combines the last two terms into $2\operatorname{Re}\langle A_t\psi',\psi\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-\frac i\hbar q\bigr)$ with $q:=\langle A_tK\psi,\psi\rangle$, and for $q=x+iy$ one has $-\frac i\hbar q=\frac{y-ix}\hbar$, so $2\operatorname{Re}(-\frac i\hbar q)=\frac{2y}\hbar=\frac2\hbar\operatorname{Im}q$. Since $A_t$ is self-adjoint, $q=\langle A_tK\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle K\psi,A_t\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle}$, hence $\operatorname{Im}q=-\operatorname{Im}\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle$ and $g'=\langle A'_t\psi,\psi\rangle-\frac2\hbar\operatorname{Im}\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle$. If in addition $A_t\psi\in D(K)$ and $K\psi\in D(A_t)$, then $\langle KA_t\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle$ and $\langle A_tK\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle K\psi,A_t\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle}$, so $\langle[K,A_t]\psi,\psi\rangle=2i\operatorname{Im}\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle$ and $-\frac2\hbar\operatorname{Im}\langle A_t\psi,K\psi\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[K,A_t]\psi,\psi\rangle$, completing (b).

[The commutator form] Since $\psi'(t)\in D(A)$ by hypothesis 1 and $A$ is symmetric [F1], $\langle A\psi'(t),\psi(t)\rangle=\langle\psi'(t),A\psi(t)\rangle$, so $f'(t)=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\psi'(t),A\psi(t)\rangle$. Substituting $\psi'=-\frac i\hbar K\psi$ and writing $z:=\langle A\psi(t),K\psi(t)\rangle$, we get $f'=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-\frac i\hbar\langle K\psi,A\psi\rangle\bigr)=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-\frac i\hbar\overline z\bigr)$; since $\operatorname{Re}(-\frac i\hbar\overline z)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-\frac i\hbar(\operatorname{Re}z-i\operatorname{Im}z)\bigr)=-\frac1\hbar\operatorname{Im}z$, this gives $f'=-\frac2\hbar\operatorname{Im}\langle A\psi,K\psi\rangle$.

[The commutator pairing] Assume in addition $A\psi(t)\in D(K)$. Then the pairings $\langle KA\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle A\psi,K\psi\rangle$ (symmetry of $K$ with $A\psi(t)\in D(K)$) and $\langle AK\psi,\psi\rangle=\langle K\psi,A\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle A\psi,K\psi\rangle}$ (symmetry of $A$ with $K\psi(t)\in D(A)$) are defined, so $\langle(KA-AK)\psi,\psi\rangle=z-\overline z=2i\operatorname{Im}z$ with $z$ as in step 2.1, and $\frac i\hbar(z-\overline z)=\frac i\hbar\cdot2i\operatorname{Im}z=-\frac2\hbar\operatorname{Im}z$, which is the second displayed form of $f'$. This proves (a).

[Timescale bound] Let $u:=\psi(t_0)$ with $\|u\|=1$ and $f'(t_0)\ne0$. [Scope and vanishing derivative] If $f'(t_0)=0$, the quotient $\tau_A(t_0)=\Delta A(t_0)/|f'(t_0)|$ is undefined, so no timescale is supplied; and nothing in the argument produces a time operator, a measurement error or an energy-time observable, since all quantities were formed from the specified curve and the two operators. This is (d).

using $f'\overline f+\overline{f'}f=2\operatorname{Re}(f'\overline f)$.

[The integrated identity] By [F6] applied to the compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ (hence $W^{1,1}$) class $g_R$, $0=\int_{\mathbb R}Dg_R=\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_R|f|^2+\int_{\mathbb R}x\chi_R'|f|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R}x\chi_Rf'\overline f$.

[Limits as $R\to\infty$] As $R\to\infty$: (i) $\chi_R|f|^2\to|f|^2$ pointwise with $0\le\chi_R|f|^2\le|f|^2\in L^1$, so $\int\chi_R|f|^2\to\|f\|^2=1$ by [F8]; (ii) $|x\chi_R'|$ is bounded by $C_\chi$ and supported in $\{|x|\ge R\}$, so $|{\int}x\chi_R'|f|^2|\le C_\chi\int_{\{|x|\ge R\}}|f|^2\to0$ by absolute continuity of the integral; (iii) $x\chi_Rf'\overline f\to xf'\overline f$ pointwise with $|x\chi_Rf'\overline f|\le|x f'\overline f|\in L^1$ by step 1.1, so $\int x\chi_Rf'\overline f\to m_2$ by [F8]. Passing to the limit in step 2.1 gives $1+2\operatorname{Re}m_2=0$, that is $\operatorname{Re}m_2=-\frac12$.

[The second identity] Applying the same construction with $\eta_R$ replaced by $\chi_R$ (so $g_R^0:=\chi_Rf\overline f\in W^{1,2}$, compactly supported, with $Dg_R^0=\chi_R'|f|^2+2\chi_R\operatorname{Re}(f'\overline f)$) and using [F6], $0=\int\chi_R'|f|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\int\chi_Rf'\overline f$; as $R\to\infty$ the first term tends to $0$ as in step 3.1(ii) and the second to $2\operatorname{Re}m_1$ by dominated convergence ($|f'\overline f|\le\frac12(|f|^2+|f'|^2)\in L^1$). Hence $\operatorname{Re}m_1=0$.

[The means] $a$ is real because $Q$ is self-adjoint and $f\in D(Q)$; $b$ is real because $P$ is self-adjoint and $f\in D(P)$. Moreover $b=\langle Pf,f\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}(-i\hbar f')\overline f\,dx=-i\hbar m_1$, and $\operatorname{Re}m_1=0$ gives $-i\hbar m_1=\hbar\operatorname{Im}m_1$, real as required. This is (a).

[The pairing] Expand $\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle=\langle Qf,Pf\rangle-b\langle Qf,f\rangle-a\langle f,Pf\rangle+ab\langle f,f\rangle$. Here $\langle Qf,f\rangle=a$ and $\langle f,Pf\rangle=\overline{\langle Pf,f\rangle}=b$ (both means real), so the last three terms sum to $-ab+ab-ab=-ab$. And $\langle Qf,Pf\rangle=\int xf\,\overline{(-i\hbar f')}dx=i\hbar\int xf\overline{f'}\,dx=i\hbar\,\overline{m_2}=i\hbar\bigl(-\frac12-i\operatorname{Im}m_2\bigr)=-\frac{i\hbar}2+\hbar\operatorname{Im}m_2$, using step 3.1. Hence $\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle=-\frac{i\hbar}2+\hbar\operatorname{Im}m_2-ab$, with imaginary part $-\frac\hbar2$.

[The uncertainty bound] By [F9] (or [F7] applied to $x_Q$ and $y_P$), $\Delta Q\,\Delta P=\|x_Q\|\,\|y_P\|\ge|\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle|=\frac\hbar2$. This is (b).

[Equality and scope] By the equality clause of [F9], equality in $\|x_Q\|\,\|y_P\|\ge|\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle|$ holds exactly when $x_Q,y_P$ are linearly dependent; given step 6.1, the further condition $|\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle|=\frac\hbar2$ is exactly $\operatorname{Re}\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle=0$ by the identity $|\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle|^2=(\operatorname{Re}\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle)^2+(\operatorname{Im}\langle x_Q,y_P\rangle)^2$ of [F9]. This is (c). No product $QP$ or $PQ$ was used anywhere: the means, the centered vectors and the pairings were formed from $Qf$ and $Pf$ only, so (d) holds.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: [The pointwise identity] At a point $(x,t)\in\Omega\times I$, [F2] gives $\partial_t\psi=\frac i\hbar\bigl(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta\psi-V\psi\bigr)$ and hence, by [F1], $\partial_t|\psi|^2=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\overline\psi\,\partial_t\psi\bigr)=2\operatorname{Re}\Bigl[\frac i\hbar\Bigl(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\overline\psi\Delta\psi-V|\psi|^2\Bigr)\Bigr]=\frac{\hbar}{m}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\,\overline\psi\Delta\psi\bigr)=-\frac\hbar m\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline\psi\Delta\psi\bigr)$, because the term $-\frac i\hbar V|\psi|^2$ is purely imaginary and $V$ is real. Comparing with [F1]'s expression for $\operatorname{div}j$ gives $\partial_t|\psi|^2+\operatorname{div}j=0$, which is (a).

[The integrated balance] Let $D$ be as in (b). Since $\partial_t|\psi|^2=-\operatorname{div}j$ is continuous on the compact set $\overline D\times[s,t]$ for every compact $[s,t]\subseteq I$, [F4] applies on the bounded domain $D$ with the constant majorant $\max_{\overline D\times[s,t]}|\operatorname{div}j|$: $t\mapsto\int_D|\psi|^2$ is differentiable on $I$ with derivative $-\int_D\operatorname{div}j(\cdot,t)$. By [F3] applied to the $C^1$ field $j(\cdot,t)$ on the bounded $C^1$ domain $D$, this equals $-\int_{\partial D}j(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS$. This is (b).

[Global conservation] Assume (c), and let $s,t\in I$ with $s<t$ and $[s,t]\subseteq I$. For $R>0$ with $K_R:=\{x:|x|<R\}$ we have by step 2.1 applied to $D=K_R$ (for $R$ so large that $\overline{K_R}\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, which always holds) $\frac d{d\tau}\int_{K_R}|\psi|^2=-\int_{\partial K_R}j\cdot n\,dS$, so [F7] gives $\bigl|\int_{K_R}|\psi(x,t)|^2dx-\int_{K_R}|\psi(x,s)|^2dx\bigr|\le(t-s)\sup_{\tau\in[s,t]}\int_{\partial K_R}|j|\,dS$, and the right side tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$ by the hypothesis on the flux. By [F5], $\int_{K_R}|\psi(\cdot,\tau)|^2\to\|\psi(\cdot,\tau)\|^2$ for $\tau=t$ and $\tau=s$, using $|\psi|^2\le g\in L^1$. Letting $R\to\infty$ in the inequality gives $\bigl|\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|^2-\|\psi(\cdot,s)\|^2\bigr|=0$. Thus the norms agree for every pair with the closed interval between them contained in $I$, proving (c).
[Unitary dynamics] By [F6], $\psi(t)=e^{-itK/\hbar}\psi_0$ with $e^{-itK/\hbar}$ unitary, so $\|\psi(t)\|=\|\psi_0\|$ for every $t$. This is (d) and completes the proof.
